name: No Plastic
line: Ten printed sheets against single-use plastic, made with GIZ.
deck: Two words, and no ambiguity about what is being asked. What the campaign left behind is the argument itself: ten A3 sheets on single-use plastic, marine litter, microplastics and who is responsible for a thing after it is thrown away.
about: No Plastic is a demand, and the demand is the name. What we hold of the campaign is the argument itself, printed: ten A3 sheets that set out what single-use plastic is, where it ends up, what it does on the way, and what to carry instead of it.

The sheets were made with GIZ, on the commission of the German federal environment ministry, and they date themselves to 2022 — by their own print file and by the single-use-plastic rules they cite. They work through the problem in order. What the term means, and how long each item lasts once it is thrown away. Where marine litter comes from, and the finding that most of it never went near the sea. What happens once plastic has broken into pieces small enough to eat. Who is obliged to deal with a product after somebody has finished using it.

Two of the ten do the opposite of the other eight. Instead of asking a reader to refuse something, they name four Indian businesses already selling everyday things without it — cutlery, chocolate, soap, floor cleaner. Both sheets state in print that this is not an endorsement of any company. The line the set closes on is an instruction rather than a slogan: refuse single-use plastic, choose a sustainable alternative. It is the nearest this campaign comes to a demand with a method attached to it.
posters_credit: Printed on every sheet: implemented by GIZ, on behalf of the Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety of the Federal Republic of Germany, in partnership with Swechha.
posters_note: The two sheets that name companies carry their own qualification, printed: “Presenting innovative alternatives to everyday items of use, few amongst various initiatives in the country. We do not directly endorse any companies and focus on awareness generation on plastic prevention.” That still holds here.

posters.title: What’s SUP?
posters.says: Defines the term, then puts a decomposition span against a bottle, a straw, a pad, a bag, a cup and a fork.
posters.alt: Poster defining single-use plastic as designed to be discarded after one use, with a chart giving each item 20 to 500 years to decompose and a replacement named beside it, over an ocean of floating litter

posters.title: Alternatives to SUP
posters.says: Six things to ditch in one column and what to carry instead in the other. Tea bags are on it, which surprises most people.
posters.alt: Two-column poster pairing six single-use items — plastic bags, packaged water, straws, tea bags, shampoo bottles — with a named reusable or package-free replacement for each

posters.title: Plastic in the Ocean
posters.says: Marine litter defined by UNEP, and the finding that most of it never went near the sea: 80% comes off land.
posters.alt: Poster on marine litter citing UNEP and IUCN: 14 million tonnes of plastic entering the ocean each year, 80% of it from land, 70% reaching the sea bed, and a million seabirds killed annually

posters.title: Microplastics
posters.says: What happens after the litter breaks up, and the waste hierarchy that answers it — prevention first, disposal last.
posters.alt: Poster explaining microplastics as plastic fragments under five millimetres, their route into salt, fruit, vegetables and packaged water, and an inverted pyramid ranking prevention above reuse, recycling, recovery and disposal

posters.title: Cause and Effect
posters.says: The sheet that stops people: about 5g of plastic eaten a week, and microplastics found in a human placenta.
posters.alt: Poster showing plastic served on a dinner plate, scaling roughly five grams eaten weekly up to twenty kilograms in a lifetime, beside a 2020 finding of microplastics in a human placenta

posters.title: Did You Know?
posters.says: Where all the plastic ever made actually went. Nine per cent of it was recycled.
posters.alt: Poster weighing annual plastic production against the weight of the human population, and splitting all plastic ever made into 9% recycled, 12% incinerated and 79% left in dumps, landfills and waterways

posters.title: Wasted!
posters.says: The only sheet about people rather than material: the informal sector that handles India’s waste, and what unsegregated waste does to them.
posters.alt: Poster citing CPCB on India generating about 1.5 lakh tonnes of waste a day, naming the more than 40 lakh waste pickers who handle it and the diseases carried by unsegregated waste, above an open four-bin segregation unit

posters.title: What is EPR?
posters.says: The one sheet that does not address the shopper. Extended producer responsibility puts the obligation back on whoever made the thing.
posters.alt: Poster defining Extended Producer Responsibility as the producer’s obligation for disposal and eco-design, drawn as a loop through production, sales, consumption, disposal and recycling

posters.title: Replace Plastic. They Did It! (1 of 2)
posters.says: Two Indian businesses selling everyday things without single-use plastic, with what they sell and how it is packed.
posters.alt: Poster profiling two Indian enterprises replacing single-use plastic — one making edible cutlery and plates from wheat bran, one a chocolate maker packaging in upcycled cotton and cocoa bean shells

posters.title: Replace Plastic. They Did It! (2 of 2)
posters.says: Two more, on household goods and cleaning — the categories where single-use packaging is hardest to avoid.
posters.alt: Poster profiling two more Indian enterprises — one selling zero-waste personal care packaged in glass and paper, one selling cleaning concentrates as capsules in a water-soluble film

aims.h: Say what single-use plastic actually is
aims.p: The first sheet spends its whole surface on the definition and on how long each item lasts. “No plastic” is easy to agree with and hard to act on, and a demand nobody can apply is a slogan.

aims.h: Name the replacement, not just the problem
aims.p: Every item the set argues against is paired with something to use instead. Refusing is half a demand; the other half is what you carry.

aims.h: Put the obligation on the producer too
aims.p: One sheet is about extended producer responsibility — the duty of whoever made a thing to deal with it after use. The rest of the set asks the shopper. This one does not let the manufacturer out of it.

how.p: The set is ten A3 sheets with trim and bleed, made to be printed and put up. It is designed for a reader standing in front of a wall rather than scrolling past.

how.h: Every claim sourced on the sheet itself
how.p: UNEP and IUCN on marine litter, the Ellen MacArthur Foundation on where all the plastic ever made went, CPCB on India’s daily waste, Environment International on microplastics in placenta. The sourcing is set in the artwork, not held in a file behind it.

how.h: Show four who already did it
how.p: Two of the ten sheets profile Indian businesses selling everyday things without single-use plastic. Both sheets state in print that this is not an endorsement of any company.

who.h: Whoever is about to buy one of ten things
who.p: The set is built around ordinary purchases — a bottle, a straw, a bag, a tea bag, a shampoo bottle, a sanitary pad. It is aimed at the moment before one of them is bought.
One sheet is addressed to whoever manufactures and sells, not to whoever uses. It is the only one that asks something of a company.
One sheet is about waste workers — more than forty lakh people in India by the figure it prints — and what arrives in their hands when waste is not separated.

done.h: The whole set survives, and it is here
done.p: Ten sheets as printed, recovered from the campaign’s own print file. The extended-producer-responsibility sheet was missing from every working copy we held until 2026 and is back in the set.

done.h: A German ministry and GIZ behind it
done.p: Implemented by GIZ on behalf of the Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety of the Federal Republic of Germany, in partnership with Swechha. That credit is printed on all ten sheets.

partners: Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety, Germany

holes.what: We hold no distribution record. The sheets exist and the print file exists; how many were printed, where they went up and who stood in front of them is written down nowhere we can cite.
holes.unlocks: A print run and a list of places, even a partial one. It is the difference between a poster set and a campaign with a reach.

holes.what: The set dates itself to 2022, by its own print file and by the single-use-plastic rules it cites. What we cannot say is when the work started, whether it has ended, or what the partnership covered besides the posters.
holes.unlocks: A start and an end, and one line on what GIZ and Swechha each did.

holes.what: Nothing measured whether the demand moved anybody. A sheet that went up on a wall and a sheet that changed a purchase are different things, and we cannot show either.
holes.unlocks: Any test at all — a count, a survey, a before and after.

invite.note: The set was made to be printed and put up. If you have a wall, that is the ask.
